extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia passages and yes/no answers.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.publisher: Google AI Language; University of Washington
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Likely yes/no questions were heuristically identified using indicator words and length, then kept only if a Wikipedia page appeared among the first five results. Human annotators then processed question/article pairs in a three-step process: judge whether the question is good, find a passage containing enough information to answer it, and mark the answer as yes or no. The dataset also includes additional yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators could mark questions as "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated Google search queries and Wikipedia pages/passages; additional yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions likely to be yes/no were filtered heuristically using indicator words and sufficient length; only questions with a Wikipedia page among the first five search results were retained; annotators selected a passage from the document instead of using the full document.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer were kept; each question was paired with the selected passage; questions from Natural Questions were kept in the train set; the final split was 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators first judged whether the question was good (comprehensible, unambiguous, factual), then found a passage containing enough information to answer it, could mark it not answerable, and finally labeled the answer as yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess quality; disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to form gold-standard labels. Answer annotations reached 90% accuracy against these gold-standard labels; disagreements were mostly ambiguous/debatable cases or annotator misunderstandings.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support natural language understanding and practical yes/no question answering by providing naturally occurring questions that people genuinely want to answer.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is class imbalanced with more "yes" answers than "no" answers (62.31% yes in the train set). Questions are also skewed toward certain topics such as entertainment media and sports.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging and requires inference beyond surface matching; question-only models perform poorly. It is limited to Wikipedia passages and naturally occurring yes/no questions, and the authors note that a future document-level version could increase difficulty and better match end-user applications.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and yes/no question answering; training, development, and testing of models; transfer learning and fine-tuning experiments.
